answer:
**The authors did not train a random forest, a neural network, or any similar machine-learning model.** Their classification relies on classical statistical pattern recognition:

- **Linear discriminant analysis (LDA)** is the main method. The paper calls it "the statistical method of linear discriminant analysis" (p. 2). It was run on the response data in Origin 2026 and SPSS v27.0 (p. 3).
- **Feature matrix:** LDA was applied to 4 signals × 7 bacteria × 5 replicates, giving 2D score plots in which the two discriminant factors account for 99.9% and 0.1% of the variance (p. 6).
- **Hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA)** was used to confirm the grouping of the seven species (p. 6, Fig. 2f).
- **Other LDA uses:**
  - concentration-dependent identification (p. 6)
  - mixed bacterial samples (p. 7)
  - live versus dead bacteria (p. 7)
  - spiked serum and clinical sepsis serum (p. 7)
- **Blind tests:** on four strains at unknown concentrations, the method gave 100% classification accuracy (p. 6).

The paper only mentions machine learning in the titles of cited works by other groups (e.g., refs. [9], [10], [36], [37], [40], p. 8–9), not as part of its own method.
question: Which machine-learning model, such as a random forest or a neural network, did the authors train for classification?
